paras: The whitecap attack on Isaiah Dillon's house was a night shooting in Franklin County, Mississippi, in mid-November 1903, in which a band of whitecappers fired revolvers into the home of Isaiah Dillon, an elderly Black man. Several bullets passed through the cover of the bed in which Dillon was sleeping, but no injury was reported. Brought to Jackson by a Franklin County state senator, the shooting was reported as the sign of a renewed whitecap outbreak that was driving Black residents and laborers out of Amite, Franklin and Lincoln counties.

Whitecappers had been active against Black residents in Amite, Franklin and Lincoln counties for some years before 1903. A Jackson dispatch said prosecutions had kept them quiet for nine months, while a New Orleans report in the New York Sun dated their suppression to a year earlier.

According to the Jackson wire of November 20, a band of whitecappers had come to Dillon's house at night 'several nights ago' and 'riddled it with bullets'. A Jackson special of November 21 placed the attack 'On Monday night', which would make the date November 16. The fullest account, from State Senator McGee, called Dillon 'a peacable, quiet old negro, who attended strictly to his own affairs' and said the attackers fired revolvers into the house, sending several balls through the cover of his bed.

None of the reports names an accusation against Dillon or a reason for singling him out, and the attackers were not identified. McGee called the shooting 'a favorite way the white cappers have of ridding the country of negroes' and said other Black residents had been treated the same way.

Senator McGhee (also spelled McGee) carried the report to Jackson, and according to the New York Sun he laid several cases of violence before Governor Longino. The whitecappers had ordered Black residents of many neighborhoods to leave, and many did, leaving Black labor scarce.

On December 2, white citizens of Franklin County's District No. 4, meeting at McCall Creek, condemned the 'shooting into houses and giving orders to the negroes' and called a county mass meeting at Meadville. That meeting appointed a committee of one hundred on 'secret work' to find detectives and opened a 'law and order fund'. Dr. A. M. Newman, the sheriff-elect, said $1,000 had been raised for detectives and that 'the negroes have been afraid for their lives'.

In neighboring Lincoln County, the Brookhaven Leader reported, two Black farmers had been assassinated near their homes. No report of an arrest, indictment or trial for the attack on Dillon was found.

The story first ran as a Jackson wire printed on November 21 in the Montgomery Advertiser, under 'MISSISSIPPI WHITE CAPPERS. Again Terrorizing the Negroes in Three Counties', and in the Birmingham Age-Herald, which spelled the name 'Dillion'. A shortened version without Dillon's name ran in the Bamberg Herald of South Carolina and the Gainesville Star of Florida. The San Antonio Daily Light printed the senator's account under 'NEGROES ARE LEAVING', and the New York Sun ran a New Orleans version naming no victim.

Dillon's full name appeared only in a Mississippi state-news column run by the Port Gibson Reveille, the Greene County Herald and the Bolivar County Democrat under the headline 'NIGHT RIDERS BREAK LOOSE' and the deck 'BLACKS BEING RUN OUT'. These papers called Dillon peaceable but treated the shooting chiefly as a cause of the loss of Black labor, and later items, such as a one-line note in the Water Valley Progress, mentioned only the outbreak. The Brookhaven Leader went further, printing the Franklin County resolutions and urging Lincoln County men to 'rise up in your indignation and might' against such crimes.

No Black-press report of the attack on Dillon was found. In February 1904 the Atlanta Independent, under 'WHITECAPS REAP WHIRLWIND', wrote that Franklin County could not induce Black laborers to come 'for love or money' and blamed lawless white men acting under the guise of law and order.

reader.title: Whitecap attack on Isaiah Dillon's house
bases: A band of whitecappers rode at night and shot into the house of a Black man as part of a campaign ordering Black residents to leave (A1, A3, A6).

Three separately written Jackson reports agree on the night shooting into Dillon's house and the bullets through his bed cover (A1, A3, A6), though A3 and A6 both attribute the story to Senator McGhee/McGee and A1 may rest on the same informant; local resolutions confirm shooting into houses in the district (A12).

accounts.label: Jackson wire (Nov. 20)
accounts.gist: Whitecappers 'several nights ago' riddled the house of a negro named Dillon in Franklin County, some bullets falling on his bed cover; notices to leave; labor scarce.

accounts.label: Senator McGhee/McGee's account
accounts.gist: On Monday night whitecaps shot with revolvers into the home of Isaiah Dillon, 'a peacable, quiet old negro'; several balls passed through his bed cover; such shooting was their way of driving Black people out.

accounts.label: Franklin County citizens' resolutions
accounts.gist: District No. 4 citizens condemned shooting into houses and orders to negroes committed at midnight and pledged to bring the perpetrators to justice.

accounts.label: Sheriff-elect Newman
accounts.gist: The whitecap organization began again about three weeks earlier; the negroes were afraid for their lives and many had left; $1,000 raised for detectives.

accounts.label: Black editorial
accounts.gist: The Atlanta Independent said Franklin County whites were reaping the fruits of the whitecap outrages as Black labor left the three counties.

framing.detail: Wire headlines 'MISSISSIPPI WHITE CAPPERS. Again Terrorizing the Negroes in Three Counties' and 'WHITECAPPERS BUSY' report the shooting flatly, ending on scarce labor.
The Mississippi state-news column 'NIGHT RIDERS BREAK LOOSE ... BLACKS BEING RUN OUT' calls Dillon peaceable and quiet and stresses the loss of Black laborers.
The San Antonio Daily Light headed it 'NEGROES ARE LEAVING' with a deck ending 'Labor Scarce'.
The Brookhaven Leader printed citizens' resolutions condemning the 'lawless acts' and editorialized that Lincoln County men should rise up and stop such crimes.
The Atlanta Independent's 'WHITECAPS REAP WHIRLWIND' blamed lawless white men for the flight of Black labor from the three counties; it did not name Dillon.
